chapter_theme: The Vidyadhara king's long reign gives him a queen, a son Arukkakirti and a daughter Sayampavai, whose beauty is praised verse by verse until kings bow to her; then, as she comes of age, spring opens over the grove with a few sayings on the wealth of the worthless.

cast.role: king of the Vidyadharas of the southern ridge
a woman who tells that the season has come
the women who tend the young princess
the Vidyadharas, subjects of the ridge
the kings who bow to the princess
bees of the spring grove, drawn as bards and guests

143.reading: Under his white umbrella the king of endless fame rules happily, and the days of his reign run to many, spent among loving women and the ornaments of desire.
143.nuance: Line 4 is hard to construe: the word division makes it unclear whether the women and the love-ornaments are the days' company or something counted among them.

144.reading: While the king keeps the wide earth gladly under the shade of his feet, the young girls' swelling breasts are bound by their mothers.
144.nuance: Lines 3-4 are compressed; the binding of the girls' breasts by their mothers is the likely sense, shown as a sign of peace in his time.

145.reading: His keen sword is feared; kings who submit in dread of it find even the honey-dripping groves turned harsh to them.
145.nuance: The sense of line 4 turns on a word division; the reading is uncertain.

146.reading: His queen Vayuvegai, a young vine of pure birth, shines on his chest like the flower-goddess on the chest of the dark Lord.
146.nuance: The simile compares the king with the Lord who carries Lakshmi on his chest, which a Jain poet uses for royal splendour, not worship.
146.event: The king takes Vayuvegai as his queen.

147.reading: The king whose elephant wears a golden frontlet becomes the adornment of his queen, who is dressed in golden silk.
147.event: The king dotes on his queen.

148.reading: The vine-like queen with lotus eyes becomes nectar to the king and, matching his nature, a feast to him.
148.event: The queen becomes the king's delight.

149.reading: While the king lives with her many days, a son is born, Arukkakirti, wearing a garland and anklets.
149.event: A son, Arukkakirti, is born to the king.

150.reading: A daughter, Sayampavai, is born, as if come down from the good world; she is so lovely that even the vine of love desires her.
150.nuance: The verse says she came down (இழிந்து) from the good world, which gives her birth a heavenly origin; it does not say which birth came before.
150.event: A daughter, Sayampavai, is born to the king.

151.reading: The red evening sky and the young moon are set beside her as measures of her radiance, and other women bow before her.
151.nuance: Lines 1-2 and the verb in line 4 are hard to construe; the sense that her radiance outdoes the moon and the sky is the likely one.

152.reading: Her hair is like a flower swarmed by bees, her eyes like carp, her brows like bows, and her waist so slight that one asks whether it is there.

153.reading: Bees feed on the wishing-tree flowers at her ear while the vines of her brows seem to bend as if pained.
153.nuance: The sense of lines 3-4 is not secure.

154.reading: Sky and earth marvel at the radiance of her eyes, as though a goddess had been born; the maiden is gazed upon with awe.
154.nuance: The verb அணங்க is doubtful here; it may mean 'stand in awe' or 'ache'.

155.reading: Her fragrance rises beyond the body-paste she wears, and her grace and modesty make the honey-dripping flower-vine droop in shame.

156.reading: Tended by her attendants, who hail her as the lady of the hill-king's ancient line, she grows, her breasts a little heavy.
156.nuance: Whether மங்கை in line 3 names the attendants or describes her is not clear from the word division.
156.event: Sayampavai grows up in her attendants' care.

157.reading: Her sidelong looks and shining teeth are called love's own guard, and her curling hair hangs loose as she looks and moves.

158.reading: Awed by her grace, the Vidyadharas think of her and long to serve her, bringing flower-clusters without stint.

159.reading: Once she is born, the kings with fierce-eyed elephants bow with their long crowns and take up service at her feet, won by the lance of her smile.
159.nuance: Her smile is likened to a spear, so kings who bow to the father's sword in verse 145 bow here to the daughter's beauty.
159.event: Kings submit to Sayampavai's beauty as if to a conqueror.

160.reading: As she grows to a woman, love's bud swelling in her, Vayantamatilakai says that the season has come for the elephant-lord.
160.nuance: The elephant-lord is not named; whether he is a suitor or the king is not clear. Whether பருவம் means the spring or the girl's age is left open; verse 161 gives spring.
160.event: Vayantamatilakai tells that the season of love has come.

161.reading: Vayantamatilakai tells the king of kings that the season has come, and the golden kongu flowers bloom as the wealth of the worthless does, which spreads no scent.
161.nuance: The king of kings addressed is not named in the Tamil; he may be the Vidyadhara king. The simile faults wealth that lacks worth, not wealth itself.
161.event: Vayantamatilakai tells the king of kings that spring has come.

claims.claim: the wealth of those without virtue spreads no good, as the kongu tree in bloom spreads no scent

162.reading: Honey-drunk bees in the flowering grove dive into the nectar, bathe in it and play with their mates in the spring king's victory.
162.event: Bees feast on nectar in the spring grove.

163.reading: Bees are shown as bards singing at the feet of the god of love, while flower-vines like women hold out honey cups and bid them drink.
163.nuance: The flowers pour as women do, so the grove acts out a feast of the god of love.
163.event: Bees praise Kaman and drink nectar offered by blossoms.

164.reading: Bees swarm over the flame-red murukku blossoms, and the sight is like fire fallen upon a dark smoky forest.

165.reading: A bee afraid that the red ashoka blossom is a blaze finds when pollen drops that it is no fire, and goes to it.
165.nuance: The bee's fear and relief show a mistaken seeing set right by a nearer look.
165.event: A bee fears a blossom as fire, finds out it is not, and goes to it.

166.reading: The cuckoo, whose mouth is sour from nibbling mango, drinks murukku flowers and sings; even the rich, once their sweetness turns, find none to come near them.
166.nuance: The likeness (செல்வரேனும்) is drawn only in the last two lines; whose sweetness turns, the wealth or the person, is not said.
166.event: A cuckoo leaves sour mango for sweet murukku flowers.

claims.claim: those who lose their sweetness lose their followers, even the rich

links.note: In 138 elephant-kings bow to the father; in 159 kings with fierce-eyed elephants bow to the daughter.
links.teaches: The homage the father wins by victory passes to the daughter by beauty alone, so the poem lets beauty hold the sway that the king's sword held.

links.note: Verse 161 likens the wealth of the worthless to kongu trees that bloom without scent; Kural 1008 likens the wealth of the unwanted to a poison tree fruiting in the town.
links.teaches: Both name a tree whose outer splendour fails its purpose, one for giving no scent and one for giving poison, so wealth without worth is shown useless in one case and harmful in the other.

gains.a: A harsher side of the image: wealth without worth does not merely fail to please, it can poison those who come near.
gains.b: A softer case: wealth may leave the others unharmed but unattended, like blossom that no one stops for.

links.note: Naladiyar 160 says the base follow the rich as their one hope; verse 166 says people leave the rich once their sweetness turns.
links.teaches: Naladiyar shows the crowd that clings to wealth and the cuckoo shows it is not loyal, since it goes the moment the taste turns.

gains.a: A reason why the followers come: wealth is their only hope, which the cuckoo's simile does not state.
gains.b: A limit: the clinging lasts only while the sweetness lasts, which the quatrain does not say.

source_issues: Verses 143-145, 147, 151, 153-158, 160-162: several lines are hard to construe because of the edition's word division and compressed grammar; flagged uncertain where the sense could not be fixed.
Verse 166 line 4 reads பிஇன்றை in the edition, perhaps for பின்றை.
